# Tool-Connected Design Environments {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."*
>
> — John Culkin, *Saturday Review* (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** John Culkin, an American media scholar writing to explain
Marshall McLuhan's ideas, observed that tools reshape how people work. The line
is often credited to McLuhan, but it is Culkin's, a small provenance lesson of
its own. An architecture tool also shapes what a method can change and what an
architect can observe. Those limits must be explicit when the method acts
through the tool.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
How can an AI-assisted study send a bounded request through slow, stateful
architecture tools and recover traceable returns without changing the
candidate, conditions, or meaning of the request?
:::

@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization hands this chapter a specific
request. The `XR-L2-CAP-A` study will compare a rerun 2\ MB L2 baseline with
3\ MB and 4\ MB alternatives. Only `l2.capacity` may change. The selected
approach uses one `SRAM-A` evaluation per capacity, followed by at most four
cycle-level attempts with `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, and `PM-A`. Infrastructure
reruns consume that four-attempt budget. The requested returns include area,
access time, cache-local energy and leakage, matched frame data, capacity
misses, and subsystem dynamic plus leakage power.

That request is precise enough to select tools, but it is not executable yet.
Each represented candidate has to become the exact configuration each tool
expects. Workload, software, process assumptions, and model versions must
travel with it. Long jobs enter queues and may wait for licenses. A tool may
crash, time out, finish with a missing report, or exit successfully after
running the wrong top-level design. Returned files may arrive hours later and
out of order.

The environment handles those mechanics. It establishes that the requested
work reached a named tool against a named state and records what the attempt
produced. It does not establish that the resulting number is a valid
measurement or that the candidate is good. This distinction separates
*execution validity* from *design validity*. The former is this chapter's
subject. @sec-feedback-verification-trust owns the latter.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Write an execution contract that preserves a bounded architecture request
  through tool-specific translation.
- Distinguish an environment, a tool wrapper, and an execution harness.
- Preserve candidate and condition identity across queues, retries, resets,
  checkpoints, caches, and several tools.
- Separate invalid requests, setup-state failures, infrastructure failures,
  partial returns, parser failures, and completed tool returns.
- Record realized cost, raw artifacts, typed fields, unclassified warnings,
  and output lineage without interpreting what the returns establish.
- Produce the Lighthouse execution record that the next chapter can examine.

:::

## An Environment Preserves Request Meaning

Giving a method permission to run a shell command does not create an
architecture environment. A shell can launch `SIM-A`, but it does not prove
that the `3MB` configuration reached the simulator, that `XR-TRACE-A` was used,
that the cache and power models match the study, or that the expected output
files exist. A zero exit status reports a process outcome. It does not identify
what the process evaluated.

Three parts divide the work:

- The *environment* is the complete tool-connected surface available to the
  study. It defines the state a method may read, the requests it may issue, the
  tools it may reach, and the returns it may receive.
- A *wrapper* surrounds one tool. It validates a request, translates the
  request into tool-specific inputs, invokes the tool, and parses the returned
  files.
- A *harness* coordinates the wrappers and records attempts, state, costs,
  failures, retries, resets, and produced artifacts.

One environment may contain wrappers for an SRAM model, a cycle-level
simulator, a cache model, and a power model. One harness keeps their outputs
tied to the same candidate and conditions.

The interface has three paths. The read path supplies the represented
candidate, fixed state, tool identities, available resources, and prior
attempts. The action path accepts only declared requests and translates them
exactly. The return path carries execution status, raw artifacts, parsed
fields, unclassified output, cost, and lineage. These paths make the
environment inspectable from both sides (@fig-environment-tool-interface).

![**A tool interface keeps request checking, execution, parsing, and recording
separate.** The wrapper validates and translates one request, while the harness
records the attempt and preserves each return status.](images/F6-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface fig-alt="An architecture question, action schema, constraints, and metric definitions enter an environment as a typed request. A wrapper separates invalid requests from tool execution. The tool path can fail, return partial output, or complete; the parser retains raw and structured output, and the harness records every outcome with cost, provenance, and execution status."}

Read from left to right, the represented question and state enter the
environment as a typed request. The wrapper either refuses an invalid request
or translates it to the declared tool path. That path can fail, return only
part of the expected output, or complete, and the parser keeps the raw output
alongside the fields it recognizes. The harness places every outcome in the
record for that attempt with its identity, cost, provenance, and status. Later
work can then distinguish a request that never ran from a failed, partial, or
complete return.

Many architecture and EDA tools expose stateful Tcl shells or text interfaces
rather than stateless APIs. A wrapper for such a tool must reconstruct the
declared state before each invocation, use the tool's error mechanism, such as
Tcl `catch`, to return an explicit status, and serialize the recognized fields.
It must also retain the raw transcript and any unclassified output. A clean
structured record is useful, but it is not sufficient if an unfamiliar warning
was discarded while the record was built.

Translation must be exact or refused. If the study asks for `l2.capacity=3MB`,
the wrapper may serialize that value into an SRAM configuration file and a
simulator parameter. It may not silently round the value to the nearest
supported capacity, change associativity to make the configuration legal, or
substitute another simulator because it is idle. Each of those choices changes
the request. A repaired or alternative request needs a new identity and another
method decision.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="One cache request, several exact translations"}
The `3MB` candidate becomes one `SRAM-A` input under `PVT-A` and, if the
predeclared routing condition permits, one `SIM-A` configuration linked to
`CACHE-A`, `PM-A`, `XR-TRACE-A`, and `SW-BASE-A`. The wrapper may change file
syntax, paths, and command-line spelling. It may not change cache policy,
associativity, the NoC, compiler, runtime, workload, or another architecture
field. An exact translation proceeds. Anything else is refused and recorded.
:::

This narrow rule prevents a common failure. An automated repair can make a
tool call legal by changing the design that was supposed to be evaluated. The
tool then runs cleanly, but the returned result belongs to a different
candidate. Request validation should catch the mismatch before cluster time is
spent.

## The Execution Contract Precedes Invocation

An execution contract fixes the relationship among the represented request,
the tool path, and the returned artifacts before the first call. It is more
specific than a tool command and narrower than the full study contract. The
study contract says what the architecture comparison is for. The execution
contract says how the requested work will run without changing that
comparison.

The Lighthouse contract makes every execution choice visible
(@tbl-environment-contract).

| **Contract Field** | **`XR-L2-CAP-A` Execution Contract** |
| --- | --- |
| **Study and request identity** | Study `XR-L2-CAP-A`, contract `CONTRACT-A`, design revision `XR-COMPUTE-A`, and the approach decision from @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization. |
| **Candidates and fixed state** | `L2-2M-A`, `L2-3M-A`, and `L2-4M-A`; cache policy `CACHE-POLICY-A`; NoC `NOC-A`; memory system `MEMSYS-A`; compiler `COMPILER-A`; runtime `RUNTIME-A`; software image `SW-BASE-A`; and workload snapshot `XR-TRACE-A` with stable frame identifiers. |
| **Permitted translation** | Serialize only `l2.capacity` values `2MB`, `3MB`, and `4MB` into declared `SRAM-A` and `SIM-A` inputs. A wrapper may change syntax and file layout but may not change architecture meaning. |
| **Tool and condition identities** | `SRAM-A` under `PVT-A`, followed by `SIM-A` with `CACHE-A` and `PM-A`. The record retains exact versions or hashes, relevant flags, host or container identity, seeds, and reset state. |
| **Execution order** | Run one SRAM evaluation per capacity. After the required area and access-time fields parse successfully, dispatch no `SIM-A` attempt for a capacity whose returned area exceeds `1.5\ mm^2^` or whose returned access time exceeds `2.5\ ns`. This approach-authorized predicate controls only the next tool call and does not label the candidate rejected. Run the shared 2\ MB baseline and other authorized alternatives under matched workload and software conditions. |
| **Expected returns** | Area, access time, cache-local energy and leakage, matched frame records, 99th-percentile frame-time inputs, capacity misses, subsystem dynamic and leakage power, warnings, reports, and raw logs. |
| **Budget and stop** | Three SRAM evaluations and no more than four cycle-level attempts, including infrastructure reruns. Stop on budget exhaustion, missing required inputs or tools, no eligible alternative, or completion of all authorized work. |
| **Failure and retry behavior** | Refuse invalid requests before invocation. Record timeouts, cancellations, license failures, host failures, stale-state failures, missing outputs, and parser failures separately. A retry creates a new attempt linked to its parent and consumes budget according to the study contract. |
| **Reset, checkpoint, and cache behavior** | Build each SRAM input from the represented candidate. Start every clean `SIM-A` attempt in a new work directory generated from `XR-COMPUTE-A` and the fixed condition set. A retry regenerates that state rather than resuming the stale directory. The initial live history is empty, so no cached evaluation return may be reused. A generated build artifact may be reused only when the complete declared build action matches, including inputs, transformation and tool versions, flags, conditions, and relevant environment state. |
| **Artifact retention** | Retain translated inputs, commands, standard output and error, reports, matched frame records, parsed fields, unclassified warnings, output hashes, and parent-child lineage. |
| **What the environment may not decide** | Whether a return is a valid measurement, whether two returns form a valid comparison, whether a physical limit establishes rejection, or whether a candidate should advance. |

: **An execution contract prevents tool mechanics from rewriting the study.**
The request, translation, state, expected outputs, failure behavior, cost, and
limits are fixed before invocation.
{#tbl-environment-contract tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Write this contract before the first tool call. Filled afterward, it merely
describes what happened and cannot refuse an invalid translation or require a
missing output.

Three parts answer different questions. The wrapper checks whether the request
matches its schema and whether translation preserves the requested meaning. The
harness checks whether the attempt reached a declared completion state and
returned the required artifacts. The named simulator, model, or signoff tool
returns the result for the property it was asked to examine. None of these
steps decides whether the return forms a valid measurement or supports a design
decision. That interpretation belongs to @sec-feedback-verification-trust.

The contract also limits scheduling freedom. A harness may choose a host,
reserve a declared license, or resume an authorized attempt. It may not replace
`SIM-A` with an analytical model, serve a stale cached result, or skip the
shared baseline simply because another path is cheaper. Those are approach
changes, not execution choices.

## Identity Survives Translation and Reuse

Architecture tools rarely consume the representation in which the study was
formulated. An SRAM model reads an organization and technology configuration.
A cycle-level simulator reads a platform description, workload image, and
model parameters. A power model may consume activity and event counts produced
by another tool. The environment must lower one represented candidate into
these forms while retaining the parent relationship.

Each transformation record names:

- the parent candidate and request;
- the transformation and tool version;
- input identifiers and content hashes where useful;
- fixed conditions inherited from the study;
- the output artifact and its hash;
- whether the transformation may change architecture meaning; and
- the next authorized consumer.

A semantics-preserving serialization keeps the candidate identity. A
semantics-changing edit creates another candidate. This distinction matters
when a wrapper repairs a malformed file. Adding a missing quote around `3MB`
may preserve meaning. Reducing the cache to `2MB` so the parser accepts it does
not.

Content hashes make exact artifacts distinguishable. They do not prove that
two artifacts are functionally equivalent or represent the same architecture.
Build systems such as Bazel illustrate how declared inputs and
content-sensitive action caches can make transformations more inspectable
[@Bazel]. Nondeterministic or undeclared tool state can still defeat
reproducibility, so the harness records the execution conditions as well as the
hash.

A larger hardware and software change makes the lineage problem visible
(@fig-artifact-lineage). The same root intent may produce several software
binaries and RTL artifacts. Changing one binary while holding the RTL fixed
creates a new evaluation instance even when the root intent has not changed.

![**Every evaluated artifact needs an identifiable parent.** Software and
hardware artifacts derived from one proposal retain their transformation
history, and a changed input creates a new evaluation
identity.](images/F5-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage fig-alt="One Lighthouse intent branches into software variant S2 and hardware variant H3. S2 compiles into binary B2, H3 elaborates into RTL R3, and one evaluation instance binds the selected B2 and R3. Identifiers and hashes distinguish exact artifacts and paths but do not prove functional equivalence or reproducibility."}

In the displayed branch, the Lighthouse intent produces software variant `S2`
and hardware variant `H3`. `S2` compiles into binary `B2`, while `H3`
elaborates into RTL `R3`; the selected pair becomes one evaluation instance.
Replacing either child creates a different pair even when the root intent does
not change. The identifiers and hashes distinguish the exact artifacts and
their transformation path. They do not establish functional equivalence or
reproducibility when relevant state remains undeclared.

One component may prepare all of these artifacts, or specialized hardware,
software, and verification roles may divide the work. The execution rule is
the same. Every tool request retains the study identity, candidate parent,
fixed system state, and architecture objective. Coordination among several
roles does not replace a shared execution contract.

Conditions need the same discipline. A return retains the conditions that
apply to its tool and marks nonapplicable fields explicitly. `SRAM-A` carries
`PVT-A`, circuit and technology assumptions, and model version. An
implementation timing or power return also carries its corner, operating mode,
libraries, constraints, and relevant flags. `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, and `PM-A`
carry workload, software image, warm-up and region policy, seed, checkpoint,
and model configuration. The return path preserves those fields without
deciding whether they are sufficient. That judgment comes later.

The host environment can also change a result. Mytkowicz and colleagues showed
that link order and UNIX environment size can perturb measured performance by
more than many reported optimizations [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. An optimizer
with many attempts can exploit such effects. Pinning and recording the binary,
host, environment, and flags prevents an accidental host difference from
masquerading as a candidate difference.

Caching creates a related risk. A result may be reused only when the contract
permits it and every identity on which the return depends matches. A cache key
that includes only `l2.capacity` is insufficient when the workload, simulator,
power model, or software image can change. A cache hit is an execution shortcut,
not permission to weaken freshness or comparability.

## Real Tools Are Stateful and Asynchronous

The familiar reinforcement-learning interface calls `step()` and receives a
return immediately. Gymnasium, a standard environment interface, supports more
than a scalar reward, but many benchmark tasks still make reset and return look
cheap [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium]. Architecture tools expose a different
operating problem. A cycle simulation may run for hours. A physical-design job
may wait in a queue, hold a scarce license, produce intermediate databases, and
fail after substantial work. Tool state persists in working directories,
caches, checkpoints, license servers, random seeds, and generated artifacts.

The harness therefore needs explicit states rather than one blocking call. The
minimal state machine includes validation, queueing, running, completed,
partial, failed, cancelled, and timed out. Retry eligibility is a separate
field. An infrastructure failure may be retryable, while a cancelled job may
not be. Neither status says anything about the candidate until the later review
qualifies the return.

The execution interface in @lst-environment-interface preserves these
distinctions.

```{.text #lst-environment-interface lst-cap="**One request remains identifiable through every attempt:** Scheduling state, terminal cause, artifacts, parsing, retry, reset, cost, and lineage remain separate rather than collapsing into one exit code."}
envelope = create_attempt(
    attempt_id, request_id, candidate_id, condition_id,
    tool_type, tool_stage, fidelity,
    configuration_id, seed, translated_input_hashes,
    retry_parent, reset_parent
)

if translation changes request meaning:
    return envelope(
        terminal_cause=INVALID_REQUEST,
        artifact_status=NOT_CREATED,
        parse_status=NOT_RUN
    )

job_id = submit(envelope)
record scheduling_state=QUEUED
record setup_status=PASSED or FAILED or NOT_CHECKED

while job is queued or running:
    record scheduling_state, queue_time, and partial_artifact_ids
    if cancellation is authorized:
        request termination
        terminal_cause = CANCEL_REQUESTED
        break
    if timeout is reached:
        request termination
        terminal_cause = TIMEOUT_REQUESTED
        break

wait until scheduler and process report a terminal state
if termination cannot be confirmed:
    return envelope(
        terminal_cause=TERMINATION_UNCONFIRMED,
        retry_eligibility=NO
    )
record final scheduler state
record queue_time, run_time, cpu_time, gpu_time,
       peak_memory, storage_written, license_occupancy

if terminal state is CANCELLED or TIMED_OUT:
    terminal_cause = CANCELLED or TIMED_OUT
elif setup check fails before or during execution:
    terminal_cause = SETUP_FAILURE
elif process exits:
    record process_outcome, exit_status, run_time, and resource_record
    terminal_cause = COMPLETED or INFRA_FAILURE or TOOL_FAILURE

artifact_status = inspect_expected_artifacts(
    COMPLETE or PARTIAL or MISSING
)

if artifacts can be parsed:
    parse_status = COMPLETE or COMPLETE_WITH_RESIDUAL
    retain typed_fields, unclassified_residual, raw_path, and raw_hash
else:
    parse_status = FAILED or NOT_RUN

return envelope(
    scheduling_state, setup_status, process_outcome, terminal_cause,
    artifact_status, parse_status, retry_eligibility,
    resource_record, retry_parent, reset_parent, lineage
)
```

A submission records candidate identity before the job enters the queue. That
ordering prevents a late return from being attached to whichever candidate is
current when the job finishes. Polling reports queue and run state without
creating duplicate attempts. Cancellation and timeout produce terminal records
rather than disappearing from the study.

The resource record is a typed vector rather than one opaque cost field
(@tbl-attempt-resource-record). Fields that the environment cannot observe
remain explicitly unreported. Human work is linked to the attempt or group of
attempts it supported because setup, diagnosis, and repair can span more than
one invocation.

| **Record group** | **Fields to preserve for each attempt** |
| --- | --- |
| **Tool and work identity** | Tool type, stage, fidelity, version, candidate, conditions, unique configuration, and seed. |
| **Attempt accounting** | Attempt identifier, terminal disposition, retry parent, reset parent, and whether the required artifacts and typed fields returned. |
| **Time** | Submission, queue, start, and completion times; queue duration, run duration, and elapsed time. |
| **Compute and storage** | CPU and accelerator time, peak memory where available, intermediate and retained storage, and host or cluster identity when it affects comparability. |
| **Scarce tool resources** | License or token occupancy, reserved capacity, and any admission-control wait. |
| **Linked human work** | Setup, intervention, diagnosis, review, and repair time, with the responsible activity or role when recorded. |

: **An attempt record preserves resource use and execution status:** Unique
configurations remain separate from invocation attempts, and retries remain
linked rather than increasing apparent sample coverage.
{#tbl-attempt-resource-record tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

@sec-data-representations-world-models requires these acquisition conditions to
travel with an architecture observation. This environment supplies them.
@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect later compares the resulting resource vectors
across complete systems rather than treating a cycle simulation, a
physical-design run, and a model call as equivalent samples.

Retries also need identity. A retry is a new attempt linked to the failed
attempt, not a continuation that erases what happened. The record states which
inputs were reused, which state was reset, which checkpoint was resumed, and
why another attempt was authorized. Repeating the same crash may establish
that the tool failure is reproducible for the same input and conditions. It
does not prove that the architecture is physically infeasible. A deterministic
wrapper bug, corrupt checkpoint, fixed host limit, or tool defect can fail the
same way.

Clean restart is not always free. Early simulation can branch from a pristine
snapshot. A long implementation flow may need a declared post-placement
checkpoint because rebuilding from source would waste days. The contract must
state which intermediate state is reusable and what changes invalidate it. A
checkpoint with unknown parent state is not a shortcut. It is an unidentified
input.

Tool isolation protects both the study and shared infrastructure. Each attempt
needs its own filesystem view, process boundary, resource limits, and timeout.
A malformed RTL candidate can otherwise corrupt a shared worktree, fill a
disk, exhaust host memory, or wedge a license process. The harness traps the
failure, retains partial artifacts, and returns control without treating the
candidate as measured.

The 1996 Ariane 5 inquiry documented what happens when a reused component
carries an operating assumption into a changed system [@LionsAriane1996].

::: {.callout-war-story title="Ariane 5 and the reused alignment module"}
**The claim.** Flight-proven inertial-reference software from Ariane 4 was
reused for Ariane 5.

**The gap.** A 64-bit floating-point horizontal-velocity value was converted to
a 16-bit signed integer under a range assumption that held for Ariane 4.
Ariane 5 exceeded that range. The conversion raised an unhandled exception,
and the duplicated inertial systems shut down.

**The lesson.** A previously successful component can fail when its operating
conditions change. An architecture harness must record the version, range,
configuration, and surrounding state assumed by a wrapper or checkpoint, then
recheck those assumptions for the current request.
:::

The lesson is narrower than the accident. Reuse is safe only when the
conditions that made the prior execution meaningful still hold.

## Execution Outcomes Remain Distinct

Tool paths fail in several ways, and one `FAILED` value cannot represent them.
Terminal cause, artifact completeness, parser status, and retry eligibility
remain separate fields. The rows below show common combinations rather than
one exclusive status value. They determine what the harness repairs and what
it hands forward, so they describe execution rather than architecture judgment
(@tbl-failure-taxonomy).

| **Execution Outcome** | **Example** | **What the Harness Records** | **Next Execution Action** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Invalid request | `l2.capacity=6MB`, missing required workload identity, or a translation that changes associativity. | Refusal reason, request identity, validation rule, and no tool invocation. | Repair or replace the request under a new identity. |
| Infrastructure failure | License checkout fails, cluster node dies, shared storage disappears, or a declared host resource is unavailable. | Attempt, failure class, partial artifacts, realized cost, and retry eligibility. | Retry only under the declared policy. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| Execution-state or setup failure | A stale constraint file, wrong top level, missing clock, corrupt checkpoint, or mismatched generated input reaches the tool path. | Setup identity, expected-state check, returned diagnostics, partial artifacts, and realized cost. | Regenerate the declared state or repair the setup. The candidate remains unevaluated. |
| Repeated tool failure for the same input | The same input repeatedly exhausts a declared tool resource or triggers a tool error under controlled retries. | Reproducible tool behavior and all conditions, without labeling the design physically infeasible. | Hand the typed failure forward for diagnosis without choosing the next check. |
| Partial return | A tool stops after synthesis but before placement, or produces some reports before timeout. | Completed stages, missing stages, raw artifacts, parse status, and terminal cause. | Preserve the partial return. Do not convert it automatically into a design score. |
| Incomplete or parser failure | Process exits zero but an expected report is absent, empty, stale, or unparseable. | Exit status, expected-artifact check, parser status, raw output, and unclassified residual. | Repair the wrapper or tool setup before using the return. |
| Complete tool return | Expected artifacts exist and parse under the declared schema, including reports that contain limit violations. | Typed fields, units, conditions, warnings, raw artifacts, cost, and lineage. | Hand the return to @sec-feedback-verification-trust without deciding what it establishes. |

: **Execution status determines what ran, not what the architecture means.**
Invalid requests, failed paths, partial returns, parser failures, and complete
returns stay separate so the next repair targets the right problem.
{#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[18,25,31,26]"}

A clean exit becomes a complete tool return only after the expected-artifact
check and parser succeed. Consider a synthesis script that selects no valid
top-level module and omits the primary clock. The process may still exit zero
and produce empty reports. The harness records a completed process together
with missing artifacts and failed setup checks rather than substituting zeros
for area, power, and timing.

Physical-design stages show why a complete return may still contain a reported
limit violation. Synthesis, placement, routing, and signoff expose different
artifacts and limitations (@tbl-eda-stage-interface).

| **Tool Stage** | **Return to Preserve** | **What Is Still Missing** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logic synthesis | Mapped netlist, area and timing estimates, constraints, warnings, and process status. | Placement, routed interconnect, signoff timing, and power integrity. |
| Floorplanning and placement | Cell and macro locations, utilization, congestion estimates, timing pressure, warnings, and databases. | Routed timing, final design-rule checks, and signoff analysis. |
| Clocking, routing, and power analysis | Routed timing, clock reports, congestion, design-rule results, power estimates, warnings, and databases. | Any property, mode, corner, or system condition outside the declared run. |
| Signoff analysis | Reports tagged with tool, library, corner, mode, constraints, warnings, and waivers. | Architecture interpretation, comparison validity, and authorization to proceed. |

: **Each tool stage returns a different kind of result.** The harness records
the stage and its conditions so an early estimate cannot be mistaken for a
later report.
{#tbl-eda-stage-interface tbl-colwidths="[23,42,35]"}

Raw logs remain part of the return. A commercial electronic design automation
(EDA) tool or a detailed simulator may emit thousands of lines. Passing all of
that text to a model is impractical, but discarding everything outside a fixed
parser is unsafe. The wrapper should return structured fields for recognized
metrics and failures, an explicitly marked residual of unclassified warnings
and errors, and both a retrievable artifact identifier and integrity hash for
the complete raw log.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The parser recognizes only yesterday's warnings"}
**The trap.** A parser keeps only known warning classes and drops every line it
cannot classify.

**The mechanism.** A new warning about a downgraded timing constraint or
changed clock definition appears after a tool upgrade. The parser produces a
clean structured record because it was never taught the new class.

**The lesson.** Preserve unclassified warning and error lines with the raw log.
A compact return should reduce reading cost without granting the parser
permission to decide that unfamiliar output is irrelevant.
:::

The same rule applies to partial returns. A placement density map produced
before a router crash may help later diagnosis, but it remains a partial
artifact. The environment records what stage produced it and what never ran.
The next chapter decides whether that artifact bears on any claim.

## Multi-Tool Work Keeps One Candidate Identity

Architecture studies often use several tools because no one tool observes
every relevant property. The tools differ in latency, modeled detail, and
returned artifacts. These are not steps on a universal quality scale. An FPGA
emulator may execute a target model much faster than RTL simulation without
providing ASIC placement or timing signoff. A circuit model may estimate SRAM
area and access time without executing the workload.

The useful comparison is what each tool consumes and returns
(@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum).

| **Tool Class** | **Representative Use** | **What It Models or Checks** | **What the Environment Must Preserve** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical or circuit model | Spreadsheet or CACTI-class SRAM estimate [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]. | Encoded equations or circuit and technology assumptions, without workload execution. | Model version, organization, technology assumptions, units, and limits. |
| Functional ISA execution | Spike- or QEMU-class execution. | Instruction and software behavior under the implemented ISA model, without microarchitectural timing. | Binary, ISA options, input, termination state, and functional output. |
| Cycle-level simulation | gem5-class processor and memory simulation. | Modeled pipeline, cache, interconnect, and memory timing under a configuration. | Workload, software, warm-up, region, seed, configuration, event counts, and traces. |
| RTL simulation | Verilator-class simulation. | Cycle behavior under the RTL and simulator semantics, without routed path delay. | RTL identity, testbench, compile flags, reset, waves, assertions, and logs. |
| FPGA-accelerated emulation | FireSim-class target execution [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. | Accelerated execution of a mapped target model. The FPGA implementation is not ASIC signoff. | Target model, FPGA image, host configuration, workload, and returned traces. |
| Implementation and signoff flow | Synthesis, OpenROAD-class place and route, and stage-specific signoff checks [@Yosys; @AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. | Properties exposed by the declared stage, libraries, constraints, modes, and corners. | Every intermediate artifact, tool condition, warning, waiver, and stage result. |

: **Tool class constrains the type of return.** The environment retains each
tool's model, inputs, conditions, stage, latency, and artifacts instead of
collapsing several returns into one generic score.
{#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[19,22,29,30]"}

Throughput changes how many candidates and conditions a study can afford to
examine. In one published configuration, ZSim ran a detailed Westmere-class
out-of-order model at 20 million simulated instructions per second, about
$200\times$ slower than the modeled core. The same study reported conventional
detailed simulators at roughly 100 to 200 thousand simulated instructions per
second [@ZSim]. FireSim reports a different regime. Individual
FPGA-accelerated target nodes can run at tens to hundreds of megahertz, while
one 1,024-node configuration ran at 3.4\ MHz for 3.2\ GHz targets, a slowdown
of less than $1{,}000\times$ [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim].

Those rates are examples, not constants for a tool class. The modeled system,
host or FPGA allocation, workload, instrumentation, accuracy, and simulation
scale all change the rate. The environment should therefore record the
observed throughput and its conditions, and a method should budget evaluations
from that scoped rate rather than from a generic label such as *cycle-level* or
*FPGA-accelerated*.

Sampling and checkpoint policy are part of that identity. SimPoint selects
representative program regions, while SMARTS supplies a statistical basis for
sampled simulation [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS]. The
environment records the chosen regions, weights, warm-up, fast-forward policy,
and checkpoint parent. It does not decide whether those choices support the
intended comparison.

ArchGym shows the value of exposing several architecture simulators through a
shared interface under controlled budgets [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. Real
project environments need additional state. Jobs wait in queues, hold licenses,
resume checkpoints, and return at different times. A common interface should
make those differences visible rather than hide them behind one `step()` call.

Chipyard provides a concrete multi-tool example. One configuration can produce
RTL for simulation, VLSI implementation flows, and FPGA emulation [@chipyard].
The fan-out is useful because every branch retains the configuration that
created it (@fig-chipyard-framework).

![**One configuration can feed several authorized tool paths.** Chipyard
generates related artifacts for RTL simulation, VLSI work, and FPGA emulation
while retaining a common configuration
source.](images/F6b-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework fig-alt="A flow diagram of the Chipyard framework. A configuration system feeds Chisel generators and the FIRRTL compiler, then fans out to RTL simulation, a VLSI flow, and FPGA emulation."}

The environment may execute independent branches in parallel and dependent
branches in order. Workflow systems such as Nextflow and Snakemake show how a
dependency graph can separate scientific intent from queue, retry, and storage
mechanics [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow; @KosterEtAl2012Snakemake]. The
architecture contract remains in charge. The scheduler may plan authorized
work, but it may not add a tool, skip a required branch, or change fidelity
without a new request.

Applicable inexpensive prerequisite checks should run before expensive
dependent work. If a declared syntax, interface, functional, or equivalence
check can reject an invalid artifact, the environment should stop that branch
before synthesis or physical implementation. This is not one universal tool
order. The study contract determines the prerequisites for each branch, and
@sec-feedback-verification-trust determines what a passing check establishes.

For `XR-L2-CAP-A`, the graph stays small. Three independent `SRAM-A` calls
precede the cycle-level branch. The shared 2\ MB baseline and each eligible
alternative use the same `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, `PM-A`, workload, software, and
condition identities. A failed attempt creates a retry edge. It does not
create another candidate.

## The Lighthouse Execution Record

To make the execution contract concrete, this chapter introduces a constructed
trace for the prospective cache study. It is an author-created teaching
example, not live project history or measurements from tools run for this book.
It reuses the hypothetical `2.94\ W` value posed conditionally in
@sec-architecture-20-ontology for continuity and adds illustrative SRAM
returns, a `2.90\ W` baseline, a `12%` miss reduction, a `2\ mW`
cache-leakage increase, one stale-state failure, and a four-attempt cycle-level
chronology. These values exercise the record. They are not predictions about
the Lighthouse design.

@tbl-lighthouse-execution-record preserves only the fields declared by that
construction and marks the rest unreported. The attempt identifiers are also
part of the teaching trace rather than identifiers retained from a real run. A
constructed execution and a complete execution record are different claims, so
the status column keeps them separate.

| **Constructed Attempt** | **Candidate and Constructed State** | **Constructed Outcome and Record Status** | **Return Included in the Teaching Trace** | **Known Cost and Lineage** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SRAM-2-A1` | `L2-2M-A` under `PVT-A`; the exact serialized input is unreported. | Execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Area `1.2\ mm^2^` and access time `2.1\ ns`. Cache-local energy and leakage, raw report identity, and parse status are unreported. | One SRAM call; child candidate is known; all other cost and lineage fields are unreported. |
| `SRAM-3-A1` | `L2-3M-A` under `PVT-A`; the exact serialized input is unreported. | Execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Area `1.4\ mm^2^` and access time `2.4\ ns`. Cache-local energy and leakage, raw report identity, and parse status are unreported. | One SRAM call; child candidate is known; all other cost and lineage fields are unreported. |
| `SRAM-4-A1` | `L2-4M-A` under `PVT-A`; the exact serialized input is unreported. | Execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Area `1.7\ mm^2^` and access time `2.8\ ns`. Cache-local energy and leakage, raw report identity, and parse status are unreported. | One SRAM call. The trace includes no `SIM-A` request and places area and access time above the dispatch limits. Parser status and the exact dispatch event remain unreported. This is a constructed scheduling outcome, not a design verdict. |
| `SIM-2-A1` | `L2-2M-A`, `XR-TRACE-A`, and `SW-BASE-A`; exact clean-state identity unreported. | Clean execution included; record intentionally incomplete. | Matched baseline frame data and subsystem dynamic plus leakage power `2.90\ W` are included. Attempt-level artifact and parser fields are unreported. | Cycle attempt 1 of 4; baseline relationship known; other cost and lineage fields unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A1` | `L2-3M-A` with stale constraint state. | The trace includes a stale-state setup failure. | No candidate return. Diagnostic and partial-artifact identities are unreported. | Cycle attempt 2 of 4. A later clean attempt is included, but retry parent, reset mechanism, and reset-state identity are unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A2` | `L2-3M-A`; one of two clean attempts under conditions constructed as matched to baseline. | Clean execution included; attempt-level completeness unverified. | Aggregate frame, cache, and power results span both clean 3\ MB attempts rather than this attempt alone. | Cycle attempt 3 of 4; exact parent, cost, and output lineage unreported. |
| `SIM-3-A3` | `L2-3M-A`; the clean repeatability attempt under conditions constructed as matched to baseline. | Clean execution included; attempt-level completeness unverified. | Aggregate frame, cache, and power results span both clean 3\ MB attempts rather than this attempt alone. | Cycle attempt 4 of 4; budget exhausted; exact parent, cost, and output lineage unreported. |

: **An execution record preserves missing information as carefully as returned
values.** The constructed cache chronology retains candidate state, failure,
successor attempts, and call counts without claiming real measurements,
attempt-level provenance, or completeness.
{#tbl-lighthouse-execution-record tbl-colwidths="[12,19,19,25,25]"}

The trace includes three aggregate values across the clean 3\ MB returns.
Capacity misses fall `12%` relative to baseline, cache leakage rises `2\ mW`,
and modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power rises from `2.90\ W` to
`2.94\ W`. The teaching scenario also declares that matched frame sequences
were used to produce an illustrative `0.3\ ms` tail-latency reduction with a
95 percent interval from `-0.1\ ms` to `0.7\ ms`. The record does not retain
those sequences or their identifiers. It also does not assign the aggregate
values to one clean attempt or identify which tool supplied the cache-leakage
difference. The constructed record therefore binds them to the two-attempt
clean-return set rather than to `SIM-3-A2`, `SIM-3-A3`, or `SRAM-3-A1`
individually.

The missing fields extend beyond cost. Exact translated-input hashes, tool and
model versions, host or container identity, seeds, job identifiers and
timestamps, parser status, expected-artifact checks, raw artifact identifiers
and hashes, frame identifiers, checkpoint identity, and the reset action are
all unreported. Wall-clock, queue, license, storage, and other resource costs
are also unreported. These absences make the constructed record incomplete
under @tbl-environment-contract.

That incompleteness is the intended Implement-stage finding. The trace supplies
three SRAM calls, four cycle-level attempts, one stale-state setup failure, two
later clean 3\ MB attempts, and total call-budget consumption. It does not
supply the complete execution record defined in @sec-architecture-20-ontology.
A production harness would capture the missing fields at submission and
completion rather than ask an architect to reconstruct them later.

The record includes but cannot recompute the illustrative paired-bootstrap
interval. It does not label the 4\ MB candidate invalid, call the 3\ MB result
unresolved, or recommend an architecture action. Those statements require
measurement qualification and comparison.

## Open Research Questions

The open problems concern preserving intent and identity while real tools run
under changing state and limited resources.

**How can a wrapper prove that a tool-specific input preserves the requested
architecture change?** Syntax and schema checks catch malformed inputs, but
semantic drift can occur through defaults, rounding, generated collateral, or
unsupported combinations.

**What reset is sufficient for a stateful architecture tool?** Working
directories, databases, caches, random seeds, license state, and host state can
survive different kinds of restart.

**How can late and out-of-order returns remain attached to the correct
candidate?** Long jobs may complete after the study has issued newer requests,
changed a checkpoint, or exhausted its budget.

**When is a repeated tool failure caused by the candidate rather than the
infrastructure?** Controlled retries can expose correlation, but deterministic
wrapper defects and fixed host limits can produce the same pattern.

**When may an architecture result be reused from a cache?** Useful reuse must
account for candidate, software, workload, tool, model, condition, freshness,
and every hidden dependency that can change the return.

**How can a parser stay compact without hiding unfamiliar warnings?** Typed
fields reduce reading cost, while tool upgrades and new failure modes keep
creating output outside the known schema.

**How should automated studies share queues and licenses with human design
work?** The scheduler must preserve study budgets without starving urgent
debug, signoff, and tapeout activity.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Preserve the request before trusting the run"}
An environment may translate syntax, schedule work, isolate tools, retry
failures, and parse returns. It must not change the candidate, conditions,
tool path, or requested meaning without creating a new request. Every attempt
must retain enough identity, state, cost, and artifacts for another architect
to reconstruct what ran.
:::

An architecture environment is more than a wrapper around a command. The
wrapper validates and translates one request. The harness manages state,
queues, retries, resets, resources, and lineage. Their shared contract fixes
what may run, what must return, and what the environment may not decide.

Execution status and design validity remain separate. An invalid request never
reaches the tool. An infrastructure failure leaves the candidate unevaluated.
A partial return remains partial. A complete return may include a reported
limit violation, but the return alone does not determine the architecture
consequence. Preserving those differences keeps repair directed at the request,
tool path, parser, or later interpretation that actually failed.

The Lighthouse teaching trace carries the constructed cache candidates and
conditions through the named `SRAM-A`, `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, and `PM-A` path. It
includes the stale-state setup failure, later clean attempts, illustrative
returns, and consumed call budget. It also identifies the reset mechanism,
exact artifacts, tool conditions, and realized resource costs as missing.
Nothing is filled in simply because a complete-looking record would be easier
to read.

@sec-feedback-verification-trust now receives the illustrative return values,
call counts, setup failure, aggregate clean-return group, and explicit missing
execution fields. It must decide which fields could qualify as measurements in
a real study, which comparisons are logically valid, what the checks can see,
and what such a result could support.
